final_proof:
Let the sequence of groups and bonding homomorphisms be
\[
G_1\xrightarrow{u_1}G_2\xrightarrow{u_2}G_3\xrightarrow{}\cdots .
\]
For \(n\leq k\), write \(u_{n,k}:G_n\to G_k\) for the composite bonding homomorphism, with \(u_{n,n}=\operatorname{id}_{G_n}\). Thus the underlying set of the direct limit \(G_\infty\) consists of equivalence classes \([x,n]\) of pairs \((x,n)\), where
\[
(x,n)\sim(y,m)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{there is some }k\geq n,m\text{ such that }u_{n,k}(x)=u_{m,k}(y).
\]
Its multiplication is computed at any common later stage: if \(k\geq n,m\), then
\[
[x,n][y,m]=[u_{n,k}(x)u_{m,k}(y),k].
\]

Suppose that the homomorphisms \(h_n:G_n\to H\) form a compatible family, so that
\[
h_{n+1}\circ u_n=h_n
\qquad\text{for every }n.
\]
Iterating this identity gives
\[
h_k\circ u_{n,k}=h_n \qquad(n\leq k). \tag{1}
\]
Define \(h_\infty:G_\infty\to H\) on representatives by
\[
h_\infty([x,n])=h_n(x).
\]

First we prove that this definition is independent of the representative. Suppose that \([x,n]=[y,m]\). By the definition of the equivalence relation, there is a \(k\geq n,m\) for which
\[
u_{n,k}(x)=u_{m,k}(y).
\]
Applying \(h_k\) and using (1) twice yields
\[
h_n(x)=h_k(u_{n,k}(x))=h_k(u_{m,k}(y))=h_m(y).
\]
Hence equivalent representatives are assigned the same element of \(H\), and therefore \(h_\infty\) is well-defined.

It remains to prove that it is a homomorphism. Let \([x,n],[y,m]\in G_\infty\), and choose any \(k\geq n,m\). By the definition of multiplication in \(G_\infty\), the fact that \(h_k\) is a group homomorphism, and (1),
\[
\begin{aligned}
h_\infty([x,n][y,m])
 &=h_\infty([u_{n,k}(x)u_{m,k}(y),k])\\
 &=h_k(u_{n,k}(x)u_{m,k}(y))\\
 &=h_k(u_{n,k}(x))h_k(u_{m,k}(y))\\
 &=h_n(x)h_m(y)\\
 &=h_\infty([x,n])h_\infty([y,m]).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(h_\infty\) preserves multiplication, so it is a well-defined group homomorphism.
